title: The Door That Opens Tomorrow
subtitle: A ship due tomorrow sends a warning today.

nodes.title: Dock Seven rings
paragraphs: The arrival board says the Wren won't reach Starport Nine until tomorrow. The empty dock disagrees. Its bell rings twice and a child's voice comes through the radio: “Don't open the door.”
Through the glass, the planet Pel glows red. A silver storm is gathering along its horizon. You're the station's youngest navigation cadet—and the only one close enough to answer.

Your hand is still on the station's school assignment: a chart of tomorrow's shipping traffic, three ordinary cargo vessels, and one late courier named the Wren. You had been worrying about whether Chief Osei would mark your work as careful enough. Now the courier's name is glowing on a radio channel that should be silent.

From a nearby repair bay comes the sound of Ren arguing with a vending machine. Somewhere down the corridor, the station's lights dim as the storm brushes the solar panels. You know the rules: cadets report odd signals, adults make the decisions. But no adult is standing beside this radio. The voice whispers again, closer this time, as if the child aboard the Wren has turned toward you.

choices.label: Record the warning
choices.detail: Keep the exact words and timing.
choices.outcome: The recording is clear. Someone on tomorrow's ship sounds very afraid.

choices.label: Call the repair crew
choices.detail: Ren knows every loose wire on the station.
choices.outcome: Ren answers at once and promises not to tell you you're imagining things.

illustration.alt: The cadet hears an impossible warning on a glowing radio.

nodes.title: No ship at the window
paragraphs: Dock Seven's window shows a perfectly empty stretch of space. The bell rings again. The station computer, TAVI, says the dock's pressure sensors report a ship—and also report absolutely nothing.
A printed sign reads DO NOT TRUST YOUR EYES DURING A GLASS STORM. Someone has underlined YOUR EYES three times.

You press your forehead against the thick glass, then pull back when your own reflection does something strange. For a moment it looks as though you are standing a little to the left of yourself. TAVI says this is a known optical effect and lists three possible explanations. When you ask which one it believes, the computer says, “None of them.”
The bell sounds through the floor rather than the air. You can feel it in the soles of your shoes. Whatever is happening outside, it seems to have learned how to get inside.

choices.label: Trust the sensors
choices.detail: Ask TAVI for raw readings.
choices.outcome: The pressure peaks every eight seconds. A useful pattern, even if it makes no sense.

choices.label: Check the outside camera
choices.detail: Spend charge on a sharper picture.
choices.outcome: The camera shows silver where the ship ought to be. You save the image.

nodes.title: Ren and the repair ladder
paragraphs: Ren meets you halfway down the corridor, swinging a wrench like a conductor's baton. “The dock bell has no power,” they say. “I personally unplugged it yesterday.”
There's only one way to reach the emergency cable: a ladder over a ventilation fan.

Ren has always repaired things by talking to them. Usually the things ignore the conversation, but tonight the station's ventilation fan gives a small grateful squeak as Ren tightens a bolt. “See? It likes me,” they say, and you almost smile.

You have known Ren long enough to spot their serious face beneath the jokes. They are watching the cable the way a pilot watches a damaged wing. If the disconnected bell has started ringing, then the whole station may be trusting equipment that isn't telling the truth.

choices.label: Hold the ladder for Ren
choices.detail: Let the person who knows the wiring climb.
choices.outcome: Ren finds an old service path and says you can count on them.

choices.label: Climb up yourself
choices.detail: The quickest way is to do it now.
choices.outcome: You copy the cable numbers before the fan starts. Ren looks impressed, if annoyed.

choices.label: Take the mystery shortcut
choices.detail: It might avoid the crowded corridor.

nodes.title: The passenger list
paragraphs: At Control, the Wren's passenger manifest is already on screen. Three scientists. Sixteen crates of seedlings. One junior pilot named Mika Vale, age thirteen.
The signature at the bottom is dated tomorrow. Even the ink scan is marked as received.

Mika is not a name you know. You zoom in on the junior pilot's picture: an ordinary face, a bright orange flight jacket, and a lopsided grin caught by the identification camera. The kind of person you might have met at a station school and argued with about the fastest racing ships.

At the bottom of the list, beside the seedlings, is an additional cargo note: LAST VIABLE PEL ORCHARD STOCK. You remember a documentary about trees that used to grow on the planet before the great dust years. The Wren isn't only delivering passengers. It is carrying a piece of Pel's future.

The manifest is signed with tomorrow's date. That should make it a harmless mistake. Instead you find yourself holding your breath. If the ship has not launched yet, then Mika has not heard the warning you are about to send.

choices.label: Compare the signature times
choices.detail: Find out whether any timestamp is ordinary.
choices.outcome: One signature is exactly twenty-four hours ahead. You circle it.

choices.label: Send the manifest to Chief Osei
choices.detail: Ask for help before rumors spread.
choices.outcome: The chief replies: 'Meet me at Control. Bring everything.'

illustration.alt: A holographic station computer displays two versions of Dock Seven.

nodes.title: The chief's question
paragraphs: Chief Osei listens to your story without smiling. “If you can prove the warning is real, I'll give you the keys to the outer mirror,” they say.
Outside, the red planet vanishes behind the first bright ribbon of the storm.

Chief Osei was once a rescue officer. You know this because every student on Starport Nine knows the story of the flood at the south hydroponics deck, when Osei kept thirteen families calm by asking them to count the lights in the ceiling. They are not easily impressed by a frightened cadet with a strange recording.

But they do not laugh. They ask three questions you hadn't thought of: who else heard the voice, what equipment received it, and whether anyone has opened Dock Seven. When you say the hatch is still closed, Osei nods as though that may be the most important answer of all.

“You have my attention,” the chief says. “But attention is not the same thing as permission. Bring me something we can verify.” The order is firm. So is the trust behind it: Osei is treating you like someone who might actually find the answer.

choices.label: Play the recording
choices.detail: Let the warning speak for itself.
choices.outcome: The chief recognizes an emergency code buried in the static.

choices.label: Show the strange data
choices.detail: A pattern is harder to argue with.
choices.outcome: Osei studies the numbers and tells TAVI to save every reading.

nodes.title: The reflection test
paragraphs: TAVI fires a tiny test pulse through the docking mirror. The reflected signal returns three seconds before the pulse leaves. The computer displays the result, erases it, displays it again, and finally says, “I dislike this answer.” The glass storm is bending more than light.

Ren has found two ways to investigate. The first leads into the station archives, where old flight maps and original mirror records may explain the impossible timing. The second leads through a maintenance airlock onto the station's outer hull, where the disconnected bell has started vibrating again.

You cannot follow both routes before the storm reaches Dock Seven. The archive is safer but may leave the physical evidence untouched. The hull could show you something the cameras have missed, but it means trusting your suit and Ren's steady hand.
Chief Osei calls once more: “Don't chase every answer. Choose the one you can bring back.” The radio crackles with Mika's voice, too faint to understand. You choose where to begin.

choices.label: Search the station archives
choices.detail: Look for the original mirror logs and the route that isn't on modern maps.
choices.outcome: You stay inside to find the evidence behind the impossible timing.

choices.label: Suit up and investigate the outer hull
choices.detail: Follow Ren to the disconnected docking bell, beyond the airlock.
choices.outcome: You step into the cold alongside Ren to see what the sensors missed.

choices.label: Use the emergency food dispenser
choices.detail: You never know what a red button does.

nodes.title: A corridor of red lights
paragraphs: Emergency strips flicker along the floor. Everyone is heading toward the shelter doors, but you need to reach the weather station.
A maintenance cart has rolled across the corridor. Behind it, a box of glass-storm sensors rattles.

At the bend in the corridor an older passenger is struggling to keep a rolling case upright. His hands are shaking. You almost pass him—your evidence matters, and every minute counts—but then you remember what Chief Osei would ask. Evidence of danger means very little if the people nearest it can't get to safety. The cart's wheel has jammed in a drainage grate, and the whole corridor is beginning to bottleneck.

choices.label: Help clear the corridor
choices.detail: People can reach shelter without a bottleneck.
choices.outcome: The cart moves, and the station crew promises to answer your next call.

choices.label: Take a sensor from the box
choices.detail: TAVI can turn its readings into a storm map.
choices.outcome: The sensor gives you a clear pulse shape. The corridor stays blocked a little longer.

nodes.title: The old flight map
paragraphs: An ancient map of Starport Nine hangs behind clear plastic. The modern docking lane is blue. An older safe passage is marked in yellow, right through the storm's thin edge.
Pilot Juno once flew that yellow route, back when the outer mirror still worked by hand.

The yellow route is printed so faintly that you have to hold the map against a ceiling lamp. Its line passes through a sector marked INSTRUMENT SHADOW, where ships used to navigate by counting radio pulses rather than staring at lights.

Near the bottom, someone has written a line in pencil: FIND THE HOME THAT DOESN'T MOVE. There are other notes beside the map, most crossed out. You begin to suspect that the bright new docking system was built to solve a problem the older pilots understood in a different way.
Behind the map you discover a photograph of Pilot Juno beside a small rescue shuttle. One window is shattered. Someone has carefully folded the picture so the broken glass doesn't show.

choices.label: Copy the old route
choices.detail: Maybe yesterday's maps are better than tomorrow's.
choices.outcome: The yellow line is now on your wrist screen, complete with its sharp final turn.

choices.label: Find Pilot Juno
choices.detail: A real pilot may know why the route was abandoned.
choices.outcome: Juno picks up on the second ring and agrees to meet you.

illustration.alt: A plotted route through crystalline ice toward Starport Nine.

nodes.title: A name from tomorrow
paragraphs: Mika's name flashes on your radio screen, but the channel stays quiet. You remember the Wren's launch schedule: the ship isn't even loaded yet.
A station bulletin announces that all courier departures are delayed by the glass storm. Tomorrow hasn't gotten the memo.

You try Mika's name aloud. It sounds strange in an empty corridor, like calling someone you haven't met through a door you aren't allowed to open. The radio does not answer immediately. Instead the ship's identification tone repeats, then drops into a hiss of distant engine noise.

TAVI suggests that a message aimed at tomorrow might arrive anywhere along the Wren's route, not necessarily in its cockpit. You think of Mika sitting on a launch pad, hearing a voice that says the ship is already in danger. How would you prove that voice was trying to help?

choices.label: Send a narrow-band reply
choices.detail: Try a private message to Mika.
choices.outcome: The channel crackles: 'Is somebody there?' You have made contact.

choices.label: Ask TAVI to keep listening
choices.detail: No point shouting into a storm.
choices.outcome: TAVI saves the frequency and uses less power than a full reply.

choices.label: Follow the museum map
choices.detail: The highlighted corridor looks promising.

nodes.title: A note in the Archive
paragraphs: Juno's flight notebook smells of dust and machine oil. One page bears a warning: THE MIRROR CAN SEND A LIGHT HOME—OR SHOW A PILOT A HOME THAT ISN'T THERE.
The next page is missing. Someone tore it out cleanly.

The archive's lights turn on one row at a time, revealing boxes of paper charts and obsolete control panels. Juno's old notebook is wedged beneath a training manual titled DOCKING WHEN THINGS GO WRONG. Its first page says that most emergencies begin with a small decision someone is certain is harmless.

You trace a fingertip over the torn binding. This page wasn't lost by accident; the paper was removed carefully, as though its owner wanted to keep one particular answer close. The remaining ink reads USE THE SHADOW, then stops at the jagged edge.

When you reach for your wrist radio, a transmission slips through the static. It isn't Mika this time. It is the sound of your own breathing, a few beats too fast, followed by a word you have not yet said.

conditionalParagraphs.text: Because you called Juno earlier, you can hear them explaining the old rescue signal through your wrist speaker.

choices.label: Read the handwritten margins
choices.detail: Juno left notes between the lines.
choices.outcome: You find a correction to the mirror's safe angle.

choices.label: Ask Juno about the missing page
choices.detail: Maybe the paper was removed for a reason.
choices.outcome: Juno admits the original mirror once led a rescue ship the wrong way.

nodes.title: The signature that moved
paragraphs: The manifest signature blinks out and returns with a new date: two days from now. Only you and TAVI notice.
'A paperwork error?' TAVI asks. It sounds as if the computer hopes you will say yes.
Somewhere behind the wall a small clock begins ticking backward. The archive's clock is still ticking forward. You listen to both, trying to understand which one belongs to the station.

TAVI asks permission to delete the impossible timestamp as corrupted data. You refuse. If somebody from tomorrow has found a way to send a warning, then deleting the evidence is the one mistake you know you cannot afford. You are beginning to understand why Chief Osei demanded proof instead of a story.

choices.label: Freeze the screen
choices.detail: Preserve the changed signature as evidence.
choices.outcome: The data is now impossible to overwrite, even if tomorrow changes again.

choices.label: Explain it to TAVI calmly
choices.detail: The computer is doing its best.
choices.outcome: TAVI unlocks a better set of instruments and stops calling you 'junior operator.'

illustration.alt: The cadet checks the mysterious message in a station corridor.

nodes.title: The missing minute
paragraphs: At the end of the archive corridor—or the outer-hull walk, if that was the path you took—the station cameras all display the same impossible skip. At 09:39 the dock is empty. At 09:41 it is still empty. The minute between them has been torn out as neatly as Juno's missing notebook page.

Ren says the mirror's motor may have recorded something that happened tomorrow and played it backward through the station's power lines. Pilot Juno, watching the data from her room, disagrees. “A captain can fly through a false image,” she says. “The danger is believing the wrong map.”

Two people who know the station are offering you different answers. The engineers want to climb into the machinery and find out what caused the lost minute. Juno wants you in her old training cockpit, where a pilot can learn to steer without trusting a single bright reflection.

There's no time to do both. You can become an investigator of the station itself, or learn how to help the Wren fly a route no modern autopilot would choose. Whichever you pick, the other answer will remain out of reach for now.

conditionalParagraphs.text: Your notebook is full of time-stamped pages from the archive. Juno's missing chart still troubles you, but the old route is becoming a real possibility.
The frost from the outer hull is still on your sleeve. Ren shows Osei the scrape on your visor, proof that the storm reached farther than any map suggests.

choices.label: Trace the missing minute through the engines
choices.detail: Inspect the station's gravity, coolant and mirror controls with Ren.
choices.outcome: You follow the electrical trail into the old engine deck.

choices.label: Learn Juno's instrument-only flight route
choices.detail: Find out how to steer the Wren through a storm without trusting lights.
choices.outcome: You find Pilot Juno and ask her to teach you the route she fears most.

choices.label: Send the standard apology
choices.detail: Maybe politeness will fix time.

nodes.title: Gravity has a wobble
paragraphs: On the way to the outer ring, your feet lift an inch off the floor. You catch a handrail before the station's gravity snaps back.
TAVI reports that the mirror's motor is drawing power from the wrong deck. Something is steering it.

The corridor rocks beneath your boots again. A cart rolls sideways across the floor, and for one impossible second a loose bolt hangs motionless in front of your eyes. Then gravity returns and everything drops with a clatter. You catch the bolt before it rolls into a drain.

Ren inspects the motor diagram. The wrong circuit isn't random; a sequence of tiny power requests has been sent from the mirror to the station's old engine deck. Each request has a timestamp three seconds ahead of the last. Somebody—or something—is walking a signal through the equipment.

If you follow the requests, you might discover where the impossible minute went. But the shelter lights still depend on those same circuits, and every measurement risks disturbing a system full of frightened people.

choices.label: Redirect the gravity circuit
choices.detail: Keep the station steady for the crew.
choices.outcome: The floors settle. You gain a little power but lose your clean sensor signal.

choices.label: Trace the strange motor draw
choices.detail: Find out what the mirror is doing.
choices.outcome: A hidden program is ordering it toward the ice ring.

nodes.title: The cold deck
paragraphs: The old engine deck is cold enough to frost your breath. A coolant pipe has cracked, leaving silver crystals across the floor.
Ren offers to patch it. TAVI says the spare battery beside the pipe is still charged.

The cracked coolant pipe is no bigger than your thumb, but the frost spreading from it has reached the lower wall. Ren kneels beside the leak, hands moving with the concentration you usually see only when they are building a new drone.

You hear a faint tapping under the pipe's rattle. A warning rhythm, four beats long. It doesn't seem possible that a coolant line could carry a radio signal. Then you remember the bell outside. Tonight, every piece of metal is part of the same strange message.

choices.label: Help Ren patch the pipe
choices.detail: A warmer station is a safer station.
choices.outcome: Ren's repair seals the leak, and the crew can stay in the control rooms.

choices.label: Recover the battery
choices.detail: Power may decide whether the mirror can turn.
choices.outcome: You carry a warm battery away as the coolant leak slows behind you.

nodes.title: The mirror's blind spot
paragraphs: The mirror camera sweeps the station's outer skin. At one angle, it shows a corridor that doesn't exist. At another, it shows tomorrow's Wren crossing the ice ring.
You have time for one more measurement before the camera resets.

On the camera feed, the phantom corridor ends at a door with a hand-painted star. You look up and see a blank wall in exactly the place the corridor ought to exist. You have walked past that wall a hundred times. There has never been a door.

TAVI tries to overlay a thermal image, but the two pictures won't agree. You can tell where the false light begins because its shadows do not move when the camera turns. Ren calls it a bad copy of the station, made by someone who has seen the rooms but not lived in them.

The phantom Wren appears for only a few seconds, and you can almost make out a face behind its cockpit glass. A person, not a symbol on a display. The thought makes the mystery more urgent than any warning alarm.

choices.label: Chart the safe angle
choices.detail: Write down where the false image disappears.
choices.outcome: The storm chart finally has a clear no-go zone.

choices.label: Ask Juno to judge it by eye
choices.detail: An experienced pilot might spot something a sensor misses.
choices.outcome: Juno confirms the safe angle, and the crew begins trusting your plan.

choices.label: Try the automatic rest chair
choices.detail: The station recommends a break.

illustration.alt: The Wren flies through the shimmering silver glass storm outside the station.

nodes.title: A hatch without a handle
paragraphs: The service door has only a keypad and a message: THIS ACCESS POINT IS CLOSED UNTIL TOMORROW. Your badge shouldn't work, but the lock briefly turns green.
From behind the hatch comes the familiar three-fast-one-slow knock.

Ren braces the hatch with one shoulder and gives you the look they reserve for equipment that has broken the rules of physics. You both hear the knock again. Three quick beats, one slow. The metal is warm to the touch.

The badge's date changes just as you lift it. For a moment your own identification photo appears older, as though a day on the station has passed while you were walking down the corridor. Then it returns to normal. You wonder whether the person on the other side of this door has already made a decision you have yet to face.

choices.label: Use the badge once
choices.detail: Try to learn what the lock knows.
choices.outcome: A future access record appears: your own badge was used tomorrow.

choices.label: Take the safe route around
choices.detail: Don't trust a door that's ahead of its time.
choices.outcome: You keep the emergency battery on the regular route and avoid the lock.

nodes.title: Ren's smallest drone
paragraphs: A blue repair drone sits on a charging shelf. Its sticker says DO NOT TEACH ME TRICKS. Ren insists this was an official safety instruction.
The drone still has the first station map in its memory. Its tiny camera points at the storm.

Ren built the drone from spare parts during a long power outage. It is small enough to fit inside a lunch box and has a habit of turning toward whoever is speaking, as if it wants to be included in conversations.

When the drone wakes, its blue indicator flashes in the same rhythm you heard in the station's strange messages. Ren starts to say that they taught it the pattern years ago, then stops. They remember teaching it three quick blinks and one slow blink because it made the little machine look happy. Maybe the storm has been borrowing familiar signals all along.
TAVI offers to wipe the drone's old memory before sending it out. Ren says no. Sometimes old mistakes are exactly what a new problem needs.

choices.label: Wake the drone
choices.detail: It can travel where people can't.
choices.outcome: The drone chirps awake. Its first word is 'LEFT,' which Ren says is encouraging.

choices.label: Copy its route database
choices.detail: A map is useful even without a robot.
choices.outcome: You save the old flight route and leave the drone charging.

illustration.alt: Ren works on a small, friendly repair drone in the maintenance bay.

nodes.title: Voices in the vent
paragraphs: The ventilation shaft carries a warning in your own voice: “The mirror is lying.” Ren hears it too, although they have been beside you all evening. You can hear the rattle of air rushing through the vent, then a softer sound beneath it: someone tapping three times quickly and once slowly.

TAVI traces two directions for the sound. One path leads to the Wren's live radio frequency, where Mika may be waiting for guidance. The other leads deeper into the mirror's memory, through a signal that seems to hold copies of the station and copies of its future.

The radio route offers a chance to talk to the real people aboard the ship. The echo route may show why the false light is so convincing, and why someone from tomorrow is trying to warn you. The two signals are drifting apart, and TAVI can keep only one in focus.
Ren asks which voice you believe: the person who needs help, or the version of yourself who already knows what can go wrong. It's an unfair question. You make the choice anyway.

conditionalParagraphs.text: Ren taps your shoulder and says they'll trust your next move. That makes the vent's strange voice less frightening.
You come from the engine deck with coolant on your gloves and a diagram of the mirror's hidden motor. The strange voice seems to travel through those very cables.
Juno's broken flight stick rests on the console. You keep remembering her advice: a bright picture can lie, but a ship still has a shape you can measure.

choices.label: Stay on Mika's live radio frequency
choices.detail: Talk directly to the Wren and help the real crew navigate.
choices.outcome: You hold the live channel open and hear Mika answer.

choices.label: Follow your own voice into the signal echo
choices.detail: Investigate the false station and the future recording inside the mirror.
choices.outcome: You tune beneath the static and hear footsteps from another tomorrow.

choices.label: Start the welcome ceremony
choices.detail: It's a little early, but it looks fun.

nodes.title: Tomorrow answers
paragraphs: Mika's voice returns, much clearer. “We're just outside the station,” they say. “I know that's impossible. I can see two Dock Sevens, and one is made of ice.”
Behind Mika, an alarm pulses in the Wren's cabin. You can hear someone counting backward.

Mika sounds closer now. You can hear somebody in the Wren's cockpit trying to silence an alarm and another voice reading a checklist with forced calm. Mika says the bright station is so beautiful that it hurts to look at. The other one is dim and ordinary. You remember the old map's warning: find the home that doesn't move.

You tell Mika to breathe and describe something they can actually touch. They choose the edge of their seat and the buckle of a safety strap. For a minute the fear in their voice eases. You have never met, but you understand that a person on the other end of the radio is counting on you to stay calm.

choices.label: Ask for the real ship's coordinates
choices.detail: Find the Wren instead of its reflection.
choices.outcome: Mika reads the numbers twice. You finally have a place to send a signal.

choices.label: Talk Mika through the alarm
choices.detail: Help them think clearly.
choices.outcome: Mika's breathing slows. They promise to stay on the channel.

illustration.alt: A cadet reaches toward a distant pilot on a flickering holographic call.

nodes.title: A copy of tomorrow
paragraphs: TAVI projects two possible arrival paths. One ends with the Wren docking safely. The other ends abruptly at the ice ring.
The computer calls the second path a 'predictive image.' No one asks whether the image came from a prediction or a memory.

The two paths don't split when the storm reaches the ship. They split much earlier, at a tiny navigation adjustment Mika will make after hearing the station's first signal. The difference is so small that the Wren's own systems call it a rounding error.

You ask TAVI whether choosing the better path will erase the warning that helped you find it. The computer considers this for a long moment and then says, “I would prefer a universe in which that is the most confusing thing we have to solve.”

Ren asks to see the map and points to an area where neither path has been plotted. A narrow passage runs behind the station's dark side, hidden from the bright false dock. It may be the only approach the storm cannot imitate.

conditionalParagraphs.text: You compare the two paths with the pulse that returned early. They fit together like pieces of a cracked window.

choices.label: Compare both paths
choices.detail: Search for the point where they split.
choices.outcome: The wrong turn happens seconds after the mirror flashes amber.

choices.label: Show the crew both paths
choices.detail: Get everyone on the same page.
choices.outcome: The crew stops arguing about whether the warning is real.

nodes.title: The second warning
paragraphs: A fresh transmission arrives from a second possible future. “Do not trust the rescue beacon,” says Mika, in a voice that sounds older by a hundred years.
Ren taps the screen. “How can there be two messages if we only have one tomorrow?”

Mika sends a photograph from the Wren's front window. In it, a silver wall of ice rises where the station should be. At the bottom corner of the image is a faint shape like a doorway. You stare at it too long and almost convince yourself that the door is opening.

The second transmission contains a single extra word in its emergency code: REMEMBER. You don't know whether the message is a warning from a failed future or a memory from a successful one. Either way, it has arrived because somebody on the Wren believed you might understand it.

choices.label: Check the new message's code
choices.detail: Make sure it really came from Mika.
choices.outcome: The code matches the Wren's emergency key. Both messages are real.

choices.label: Tell Mika about the contradiction
choices.detail: They deserve to know the whole danger.
choices.outcome: Mika says they'll watch for the false beacon and tell the captain.

choices.label: Put on the ancient test helmet
choices.detail: It might shield you from the storm.

nodes.title: The seedling crate
paragraphs: A cargo display shows a crate of rare Pel seedlings aboard the Wren. One holds the last living seeds of a tree lost from the planet's surface.
The crate's heat sensor is linked to the same guidance frequency as the docking mirror. That seems like an odd coincidence.

You remember the school garden on Starport Nine, where every student is assigned a tiny plant to keep alive through the dark weeks. Ren once watered theirs with a cup of orange soda and was banned from the greenhouse for a month.

The Pel seedlings are not a school experiment. They carry the genes of trees that disappeared when the planet's rivers dried. If the Wren fails to reach the station, the scientists may lose their only chance to grow them again. Mika tells you there is a small handwritten note strapped to the cargo box: FOR THE FIRST RAIN.

For the first time tonight, the ship isn't simply a problem to solve. It carries people and a promise. You find yourself hoping there is a way to save both without pretending the danger is smaller than it is.

choices.label: Inspect the cargo signal
choices.detail: A crate shouldn't talk to a guidance beacon.
choices.outcome: The sensor is transmitting a tiny pulse—perfect for marking the real ship.

choices.label: Ask Mika to secure the seedlings
choices.detail: Protect the cargo while the ship maneuvers.
choices.outcome: Mika promises to strap down the crate before the final approach.

illustration.alt: Precious glowing seedlings sit protected in a spacecraft cargo case.

nodes.title: The ice ring
paragraphs: The Wren is close enough that you can see ice fragments spin around the station like pale feathers. Every fragment reflects the dock lights.
A single wrong flash could trick the ship into turning toward empty space.

Each ice fragment catches the station light and returns a tiny copy of Dock Seven. Seen together, the shards make a whole city of false harbors, bright enough to tempt any tired pilot. Mika's voice grows quiet. They are trying not to look.

TAVI suggests extinguishing every unnecessary lamp. Chief Osei worries that the station's own shelters may need those lights if the storm worsens. The room falls silent. It is easy to say that nobody should make a dangerous choice until you have to choose which people you are protecting.
Through the window, one ice shard slowly turns and the mirror makes a thousand tiny stars. The old flight route—dark, narrow, and unremarkable—suddenly looks more beautiful than all of them.

choices.label: Measure the gaps between fragments
choices.detail: Find a corridor with fewer false reflections.
choices.outcome: You plot a narrow route through the brightest part of the storm.

choices.label: Turn off the outer work lights
choices.detail: Stop the reflections multiplying.
choices.outcome: The station darkens, but its emergency battery holds.

nodes.title: The broken translator
paragraphs: The docking console translates Mika's latest distress message into an order: OPEN HATCH. TAVI checks the original signal, then makes a small electronic sound of embarrassment. The message actually says HOLD POSITION. A software error copied into years of navigation updates has reversed two symbols.

Chief Osei calls the bridge crew together. They want everyone to hear the same warning and agree on a single plan. Ren argues there is another option: an emergency passage beneath Dock Seven leads directly to the mirror's manual control. It might let you fix the problem before the council finishes debating.

You know what the chief will say. People survive emergencies when they work together and understand the risks. But the storm is now only minutes away from the dock, and TAVI's countdown is faster than the crew's conversation.

Either way, you need to stop trusting the automatic translator. You can take the evidence to the crew and build a shared plan, or go with Ren to the machinery and try to change the signal yourself. You cannot do both in time.

conditionalParagraphs.text: Mika is still on your live channel, listening for a decision. Their voice makes the danger immediate: a real person is waiting at the end of your words.
You carry a recording of the false station's second clock. The echo showed you how convincing an invented dock can look, and how little brightness proves.

choices.label: Build a plan with Chief Osei's bridge crew
choices.detail: Fix the interpretation and bring everyone together before the last approach.
choices.outcome: You carry the corrected code to the council in Control.

choices.label: Go with Ren beneath the emergency shutter
choices.detail: Find the physical mirror switch instead of waiting for the crew to agree.
choices.outcome: Ren opens the maintenance ladder beneath the dock.

choices.label: Enable demonstration mode
choices.detail: Maybe the display will show more detail.

illustration.alt: The station AI shows two overlapping versions of Dock Seven.

nodes.title: The captain's rule
paragraphs: Chief Osei gives you an orange clearance card. “A cadet can recommend a course,” they say. “But this time you're the one who has seen everything.”
They promise to back your decision if you can explain the risks.

Osei's clearance card is warm from the chief's pocket and slightly bent at one corner. It feels surprisingly ordinary for an object that can change the course of a ship. Beside the bridge window, the crew has gathered around the two docking charts in a rough circle.
The chief does not ask whether you are brave. They ask what you know, what you suspect, and what you are prepared to risk if you are wrong. You realize those are three different questions.
Ren stands across the room beside a toolbox, and Juno watches from the doorway. Neither offers you an easy answer. For once, the grown-ups are waiting to hear yours.

conditionalParagraphs.text: Osei remembers the evidence you showed them at the start. They don't ask you to prove it twice.

choices.label: Explain every risk aloud
choices.detail: Everyone should understand what could go wrong.
choices.outcome: The bridge crew agrees to follow a single plan.

choices.label: Use the card to unlock the mirror
choices.detail: You'll need the control before the storm peaks.
choices.outcome: The mirror accepts your badge. A manual override appears.

nodes.title: Two maps, one destination
paragraphs: On the wall, Juno's paper map and TAVI's projected map refuse to line up. They agree on the planet, the station, and the ice—but not on the dock itself.
You realize one map is showing where the dock will be tomorrow.

Juno lays her old paper chart over the glowing projection and smooths the corners with both hands. The two maps agree on the red planet, the ice ring, and the station's shadow, but the blue dock symbol seems to float an inch from the paper.

She explains that the map was drawn by pilots who navigated using gravity and radio pulses. The new map was drawn by computers trained to follow the brightest guide light. Both systems work perfectly on ordinary days. This is not an ordinary day.

When you shift the paper so the stars line up instead of the docks, a narrow path appears between the ice fragments. It is not on any automated list of safe approaches. Nobody has flown it in years, but it may be the only route that keeps the Wren away from the mirror's lie.

choices.label: Combine the two maps
choices.detail: Make one route that accounts for both days.
choices.outcome: The safe path passes behind the station's shadow, not through the bright ice.

choices.label: Give Juno the pen
choices.detail: Let someone experienced draw the route.
choices.outcome: Juno finds an older approach line. The crew agrees to follow it.

illustration.alt: An illuminated safe route winds between huge ice crystals.

nodes.title: A vote in Control
paragraphs: The crew gathers around the main console. Some want to shut the mirror off. Others want to send a rescue signal through it.
Ren reminds everyone that tomorrow's crew can hear what you do today.

The vote begins badly. One engineer wants to shut the mirror down; another wants to flood the ring with warning lights. Juno says neither will help a pilot who cannot distinguish the station from its reflection.

You remember Osei's flood story and ask everyone to stop talking for ten seconds. Nobody likes the request, but the chief supports it. In the quiet you can hear the Wren's captain breathing through the open channel. They are listening, too.

One by one, the crew starts naming what each plan protects and what it risks. You write the answers where everyone can see them. Suddenly the problem is still difficult, but it no longer feels impossible to discuss.

choices.label: Ask everyone to agree on one signal
choices.detail: Keep the plan simple enough to work.
choices.outcome: The votes settle. For once, no one is talking over anyone else.

choices.label: Write a procedure on the screen
choices.detail: A shared checklist keeps surprises small.
choices.outcome: TAVI adds the safe-angle calculation and marks the dangerous switches.

choices.label: Step inside the chronology booth
choices.detail: It says TIME MACHINE in big letters.

nodes.title: The trade with time
paragraphs: TAVI has a proposal: send one strong signal now, and the Wren might never have to send its warning tomorrow. The price is half the station's spare power.
There is also a weaker signal. It won't change tomorrow, but it might guide the ship away from the ice.

The strong signal would burn through most of the spare power and might reach the Wren before the ship sends its first warning. TAVI calls this a time-loop correction, then admits it cannot explain what happens to the memory of a message that never needed to exist.
Ren calls it expensive electricity with very good intentions. The smaller signal leaves the station safer but gives the Wren less information. Neither plan is a free victory.
You imagine the families waiting under the emergency lights and Mika waiting in the cockpit. Choosing where the power goes means choosing who will have to trust someone else in the dark.

choices.label: Prepare the strong signal
choices.detail: Spend power to change the future itself.
choices.outcome: The capacitor glows blue. TAVI calls it 'a very hopeful gamble.'

choices.label: Save the station's charge
choices.detail: A smaller plan can still be a good one.
choices.outcome: You keep the emergency circuit stable and mark the weaker signal frequency.

nodes.title: TAVI's impossible question
paragraphs: “If you warn tomorrow's crew and they never need to warn us,” TAVI asks, “who sent the first message?”
Nobody has an answer. The computer asks you to choose whether that matters more than the people aboard the Wren.

The question hangs over Control longer than anyone expects. If the warning prevents the accident, the Wren may never send it. If the warning is never sent, you may never know to prevent the accident. It is the kind of puzzle that sounds fun in a classroom and terrible when real people are involved.
Osei comes to stand beside you. “You don't have to solve time,” the chief says quietly. “You have to make a good decision with the information you have.” You try to hold onto that distinction.

TAVI opens its earliest memory of the docking mirror. Hidden beneath decades of routine logs is a recording made by a cadet who sounds almost like you. The recording ends with the same four-note knock. You wonder if the station has been waiting a long time for somebody to listen.

choices.label: Say the people matter most
choices.detail: The mystery can wait.
choices.outcome: TAVI seems relieved and assigns the rescue team to your plan.

choices.label: Find the first signal's source
choices.detail: Understanding the loop may help close it.
choices.outcome: The signal begins in the mirror's own memory bank.

illustration.alt: TAVI projects an impossible view of the dock across two timelines.

nodes.title: The silent bell
paragraphs: The dock bell stops ringing. For the first time since the warning arrived, the station is quiet enough to hear the ventilation fans turn. On the main screen, the Wren is making its last approach. The glass storm has swallowed the outer ice ring and begun painting bright false docks across the sky.

Chief Osei lays out the final options. You can stay in Control, coordinate a careful blue-light signal with Mika and the entire bridge crew, and try to guide the Wren to the true dock. Or you can join Ren at the outer mirror's manual control, where a physical adjustment may cut through the interference but carries the risk of damaging the station.

The first plan relies on people following one shared rhythm. The second relies on machinery you can touch and a decision you might have to make without the crew beside you. There is not enough time to prepare both. Osei asks you to choose one.
Mika's voice comes through the radio: “Whatever you do, please tell us before you do it.” You promise you will. Then you decide where to spend the last minutes before tomorrow arrives.

conditionalParagraphs.text: You can hear the bridge crew behind you repeating the revised instructions. They understand the risk because you let them argue through it together.
The metal of Ren's override key presses against your palm. You found a way to move the mirror, but you also know how much the station might pay if you move it wrong.

choices.label: Coordinate a careful blue-light signal
choices.detail: Stay with the crew and synchronize a signal with Mika's cockpit.
choices.outcome: The bridge clears the channel. You prepare one shared pulse.

choices.label: Take the manual mirror-rescue route
choices.detail: Bring Ren to the hidden mirror controls and adjust the signal yourself.
choices.outcome: You go below the shutter for the last manual rescue attempt.

choices.label: Ask the help desk to solve the storm
choices.detail: They promised twenty-four-hour support.

nodes.title: Seal or signal
paragraphs: A safety shutter closes over the end of Dock Seven. The station's protection system wants every door shut for the glass storm.
To send a rescue signal, someone will need to route it around that shutter.

The service antenna was built when Starport Nine had only a handful of residents and everyone knew which switch did what. Its cables are painted with names instead of numbers. Ren recognizes one label from an old repair manual, then reaches through a maintenance gap to test the line.

Osei tells the shelter crew to stay clear of Dock Seven. You imagine the families waiting behind sealed doors and find yourself grateful that someone is making the ordinary safety decisions while you chase the impossible ones.
Beyond the glass, the Wren's lights vanish behind a silver ribbon. When they reappear, there are two sets. You have to keep reminding yourself that the brighter set is not necessarily real.

choices.label: Route the signal through the old antenna
choices.detail: A longer path, but no need to open the dock.
choices.outcome: You find a clean channel to the Wren.

choices.label: Hold the shutter for a moment
choices.detail: Let the crew prepare the signal equipment.
choices.outcome: The crew makes room in the service corridor before the shutter comes down.

nodes.title: The last battery
paragraphs: Only two power cells remain in the console. One runs the outer mirror. The other keeps the emergency lights on in the station shelters.
Ren says you can take a cell from the antenna, but the climb will cost a minute.
The battery cell is heavier than it looks. Ren lifts it onto a bench and checks the indicator twice, as if a second look might make the charge last longer. The power meter continues to fall.

You can hear the station's shelter lights clicking on in the background. Every time the Wren sends a transmission, the mirror draws another pulse from the emergency circuit. The problem feels less like a number and more like a room full of people counting on you not to spend their last light.
Ren asks whether they should fetch another cell from the cold deck. There isn't time. You work with what is already in front of you.

choices.label: Leave shelter power untouched
choices.detail: People on the station come first.
choices.outcome: The emergency lights stay on. You find a smaller charge you can spare.

choices.label: Borrow the antenna cell
choices.detail: Take the risk yourself instead of darkening shelters.
choices.outcome: You get one extra pulse for the mirror's motor.

illustration.alt: The cadet studies a warning signal's orange waveform.

nodes.title: The reflection window
paragraphs: A shape slides across the glass: a ship with the Wren's silhouette, except its engines are dark. Its reflection moves in the wrong direction.
TAVI labels it ECHO, not SHIP. You press your palm against the cold window.

The false ship passes so close to the docking window that you can see a row of little squares where its windows should be. Behind one of those squares a figure raises a hand. Then the whole image slides sideways and vanishes into an ice shard.

Ren doesn't see the figure. They see the station crew watching you, waiting to learn whether the bright shape can be trusted. You choose your words carefully. It is hard to tell someone you have seen something impossible without making them afraid of every ordinary thing around them.

conditionalParagraphs.text: You recognize the dangerous silver curve from your earlier measurements. The false ship is following it exactly.

choices.label: Mark the echo's position
choices.detail: Keep the false ship out of your route.
choices.outcome: The echo's path gives you an exact angle to avoid.

choices.label: Warn Mika about the false shape
choices.detail: No one aboard should mistake it for home.
choices.outcome: Mika agrees to follow your voice rather than the bright outline.

choices.label: Try the emergency escape pod
choices.detail: You want another angle on the storm.

nodes.title: A pulse of silver
paragraphs: The storm is almost touching the mirror. A single burst of light can cut through it, but it may also make every piece of ice shine like a tiny false dock.
Your wrist radio vibrates. Mika is waiting.

TAVI reduces every display to a single waveform and a simple blue line. No bright arrows, no helpful animations, no automatic suggestions. For the first time, the station's technology seems to be listening rather than insisting it knows best.

Mika taps three times quickly and once slowly. You answer with the same rhythm. The signal crosses the storm, and the Wren answers again. It is such a small exchange that you could almost miss how important it is: two people agreeing that they are talking to each other, not to a reflection.
Chief Osei moves closer to the console but does not take it away from you. “Tell us when,” the chief says. All the voices on the bridge go quiet. You have never felt a room become so still.

choices.label: Synchronize the pulse with Mika
choices.detail: One shared count could keep both crews together.
choices.outcome: Mika whispers 'ready' and taps the same rhythm as your heart.

choices.label: Choose the measured frequency
choices.detail: The chart tells you where the light will go.
choices.outcome: Your waveform matches the map exactly. TAVI approves for the first time today.

illustration.alt: The Wren's suggested flight path winds through dangerous crystalline ice.

nodes.title: The crew on the other side
paragraphs: You hear the Wren's captain give an order, and then Mika says, “We can see your station. For a second we can see it twice.”
Osei places a hand on the console. Nobody will take the decision away from you now.

Through the open channel you hear the Wren's captain explain the plan back to the crew. There is a little uncertainty in their voice, and you are relieved by it. They are not pretending to know more than they do.

Mika repeats the route with the careful concentration of someone threading a needle in the dark. You repeat each turn as if it were the only important thing in the universe. Ren stands by the manual safety switch in case the mirror moves unexpectedly.

At the edge of the screen, the false docking marker begins to fade. You don't know whether you are saving the ship, rewriting tomorrow, or doing both. You know only that the people aboard the Wren are still answering.

choices.label: Send Mika your final route
choices.detail: Give the Wren a plan they can execute.
choices.outcome: Mika repeats the safe coordinates without a mistake.

choices.label: Ask the bridge crew to repeat your plan
choices.detail: Make sure everyone knows what will happen next.
choices.outcome: Three voices repeat the signal timing back to you.

nodes.title: No more warnings
paragraphs: The warning lights go steady. A calm voice says the Wren has reached the last approach point. The station can send one final command.
You remember the first message: DON'T OPEN THE DOOR. It never said not to turn on the light.

The first voice you heard today returns over the radio. This time you recognize Mika's breathing, the soft hum of the cockpit, and the captain's quiet instruction to hold position. The warning no longer sounds like a mystery. It sounds like someone trying very hard to keep another person safe.

You think of the different places the day might have taken you: a dusty archive, the cold outside rail, an old pilot's simulator, a doubled signal, the crowded bridge, or a hidden motor beneath the shutter. Not all of those places could fit into a single day. The choices you made determine which evidence and allies you brought here.
Whatever happens next, you won't be able to take this decision back. The emergency hatch is sealed. Beyond it, the bright reflection waits. The real ship is somewhere behind the ice.

conditionalParagraphs.text: Mika says your name over the radio. You don't remember giving it to them, but the sound keeps you steady.
A blue waveform is waiting on the console, clean and simple. You and Mika have a chance to answer one another at exactly the right instant.
The emergency crank still hums through the wall. You know how to move the mirror by hand, and you know its old motor could break if you ask too much.

choices.label: Check every safety lock
choices.detail: Make sure no door opens by accident.
choices.outcome: All pressure doors remain sealed. The only thing you can change is the guide light.

choices.label: Tell Ren to guard the hatch
choices.detail: Someone should keep an eye on it.
choices.outcome: Ren gives you a two-finger salute and bolts the manual latch.

choices.label: Run the automatic victory test
choices.detail: Check whether the plan is good enough.

illustration.alt: The Wren approaches the station through the glass storm.

nodes.title: A very final broom closet
paragraphs: You pull the handle labeled EMERGENCY EXIT. The door swings inward. Beyond it is a broom closet, complete with a mop that falls dramatically onto your shoe.

nodes.title: The heroic snack break
paragraphs: You press CREW EMERGENCY and a tray of hot noodles arrives from the cafeteria. The crew is grateful. The Wren, sadly, is still in danger.

nodes.title: A map of the wrong station
paragraphs: You unfold the map marked SECRET ROUTE. It is a guide to the museum's model of Starport Nine. After three turns, you are standing in front of a very small plastic dock.

ending.title: THE END (OF THIS MAP)
ending.note: A real map would help more.

nodes.title: The automatic apology
paragraphs: The computer offers to apologize to tomorrow for the delay. You accept. It sends SORRY ABOUT THE WEATHER four thousand times and fills the message screen.

ending.title: THE END (OF THE INBOX)
ending.note: Cancel the apology and try again.

nodes.title: The twelve-second nap
paragraphs: A medical chair promises a quick rest. You sit. It locks into overnight recovery mode and begins playing whale songs. Ren pulls the plug before you fall asleep.

ending.title: THE END (OF YOUR NAP)
ending.note: You have a ship to save.

nodes.title: The victory parade
paragraphs: You press the green control marked CELEBRATE ARRIVAL. Confetti pours from the ceiling. The Wren has not arrived, but TAVI plays a trumpet fanfare anyway.

nodes.title: The spectacularly wrong helmet
paragraphs: The locker opens to reveal a helmet the size of a fishbowl. When you put it on, every voice sounds like a duck. Ren takes a picture for blackmail.

nodes.title: An upgrade nobody asked for
paragraphs: The mirror's software offers DELUXE DEMONSTRATION MODE. You agree. Every docking arrow becomes a dancing cartoon star. TAVI refuses to continue until you undo it.

nodes.title: The wrong kind of time machine
paragraphs: You step inside the archive's chronology booth. It stamps today's date on a paper wristband. That's all it does. The attendant asks whether you want a souvenir.

nodes.title: A rather permanent hold tune
paragraphs: You call the station's help line. It puts you on hold. At least the music is pleasant. TAVI estimates a six-month wait for an operator.

ending.title: THE END (OF THE CALL)
ending.note: Hang up before the next song.

nodes.title: The brave escape pod
paragraphs: You enter the escape pod to inspect the windows. A voice announces, 'This pod is decorative.' The door opens onto a gift shop.

nodes.title: The fake finish line
paragraphs: The console flashes YOU HAVE WON and plays a little tune. The letters below say TRAINING SIMULATION COMPLETE. The actual Wren is still waiting outside.

ending.title: THE END (OF THE TRAINING)
ending.note: The real final call is still ahead.

nodes.title: Your call, cadet
paragraphs: The Wren reaches its last approach point. The glass storm fills the window like a wall of silver paper, folding and unfolding around a little ship that appears in three places at once. On the station's main screen, one docking lane remains bright and easy. Another disappears into shadow. The third is visible only as a thin blue pulse.

Your choices have brought you different people, knowledge, and tools. A trained pilot's route might let the ship fly around the danger. A synchronized signal may bring it through the storm and close the time loop, but only if you built enough trust, gathered enough evidence, and still have the power. A manual override may get the ship home at a cost to the station. You can also protect the dock by turning the Wren away.

Chief Osei does not tell you which answer to choose. Ren waits beside the emergency cutoff. From the open radio comes Mika's voice, smaller now than when you first heard it: “I can see the light. I don't know which one is yours.”

You remember the first warning, and the sound of a hand knocking three times quickly and once slowly. The answer you give Mika will decide more than where the Wren lands. It will decide which tomorrow is allowed to happen.

conditionalParagraphs.text: You remember Mika's counted pulse. It could connect the real ship to the real dock.

choices.label: Send the true route together
choices.detail: Guide the Wren with the corrected light and both crews in sync.
choices.outcome: The blue light reaches both days at once.

requirements.hint: Talk to Mika on the live channel
Build a plan with the bridge crew

choices.label: Guide the Wren around the ice
choices.detail: Take the long approach, even if the time loop stays unsolved.
choices.outcome: The ship follows the older map, slowly and carefully.

requirements.hint: Train with Juno on the old flight route

choices.label: Force the old mirror into position
choices.detail: Use the reserve charge for one risky flash.
choices.outcome: The mirror moves with a grinding cry.

requirements.hint: Find and prepare the manual mirror override

choices.label: Close the guide lights and delay arrival
choices.detail: Keep the station safe, but turn away the Wren.
choices.outcome: The bridge shutters darken the stars.

choices.label: Open the main hatch and follow the brightest light
choices.detail: Ignore the warning and trust the easiest-looking path.
choices.outcome: The bright line across the ice is not a docking lane.

illustration.alt: The station's glowing AI interface displays two possible futures.

nodes.title: Tomorrow arrives safely
paragraphs: You count with Mika: three fast beats, one slow. The outer mirror answers in the exact rhythm you measured, and the ice ring goes dark for one perfect second.
Through the silver storm, the Wren's real lights appear. Not a reflection. Not a memory. Chief Osei guides the ship into Dock Seven without opening the hatch until the pressure display reads SAFE.

The next morning the Wren arrives on schedule anyway. Mika steps off carrying the first Pel seedling and says, “I think we fixed tomorrow yesterday.” TAVI suggests that this sentence is illegal in several branches of mathematics.
The station's old mirror is rebuilt. The seedlings will grow. Ren keeps the note you wrote during the storm and tapes it above the new console: BELIEVE THE SIGNAL. CHECK THE LIGHT.

In the days that follow, Juno helps you compare the old yellow flight map with the station's new records. Some of the ink has changed. A path that used to end at an ice shard now curves neatly into Dock Seven. You keep both versions, because a solved mystery can still be worth remembering.

Mika visits the little greenhouse where the seedlings are planted. Each person who helped with the rescue writes their name on a tag and ties it beside the first tree. Yours is one of the smallest tags. It doesn't need to be bigger. When the station bell rings for the next incoming ship, you smile instead of reaching for the emergency radio.

ending.title: Tomorrow arrives safely
ending.note: BEST OUTCOME · Everyone arrives, and the time loop is closed.

illustration.alt: A steady blue signal guides the Wren safely toward the starport.

nodes.title: The long way home
paragraphs: You choose the older approach route, away from the sharpest ice. Mika repeats the bearings, and the Wren turns into the dark shadow behind the station.
It takes almost a full day to reach the dock. No one complains. When the Wren finally lands, its passengers are tired and hungry, but unharmed. The seedlings survive the delay.
The first warning remains on your wrist radio, though nobody remembers sending it. Chief Osei calls this a mystery worth keeping. TAVI calls it a flaw in the universe's filing system.
Mika asks to see the glass storm from the observation deck. You stand beside them and watch a silver ribbon fade into space.

At the celebration, Juno tells the Wren's captain that she once abandoned the yellow route because it reminded her of a bad day. Now she is teaching it again. Mika asks whether they can study with her, and Juno pretends to consider the request for several minutes before saying yes.

Your old recording still plays the warning from tomorrow. You listen to it with Ren as the planet Pel turns slowly beneath the window. Neither of you tries to explain the impossible signal. You have learned that some questions deserve an answer and some deserve a little patience.

ending.title: The long way home
ending.note: GREAT OUTCOME · Everyone is safe, but the mystery remains.

illustration.alt: The Wren finds a safer path around the storm and returns toward the station.

nodes.title: A hard landing
paragraphs: You swing the old mirror into position using the reserve cells. For one breathless moment the signal vanishes. Then the Wren shoots out of the silver fog at a dangerous angle.
The docking clamps catch the ship just in time. The Wren's crew gets out safely, with the seedling crates mostly intact. But the outer mirror snaps in half and the station loses power to three decks.
Ren spends the next week helping repair Starport Nine. Chief Osei thanks you for making the dangerous choice that brought the Wren home, then points out the long list of repairs it caused.
Mika finds you under the broken mirror and says, “Next time, maybe we use the long way around.” You agree. Next time you'll know more.

Several decks remain closed while the engineers make repairs. You help Ren carry tools through the long dark corridors, listening to the steady tap of a wrench where the station's regular sounds ought to be. You see exactly what your decision cost.

Osei puts the repair bill beside the Wren's safe-arrival report. “Both of these are part of the result,” the chief says. You keep a copy of each. Mika asks to help repaint the cracked mirror housing, and Ren finally lets someone else hold the ladder.
The station recovers. So do the seedlings. But you know now that an ending can be good for one group of people and still leave another with the work of making things whole.

ending.title: A hard landing
ending.note: MIXED OUTCOME · The crew survives, but Starport Nine pays the price.

illustration.alt: A dangerous flight path threads through bright ice crystals.

nodes.title: The empty docking bay
paragraphs: You darken the guidance lights and seal the dock. The false reflections disappear. So does the Wren's reply.

For two terrible hours there is no voice on the radio. Then another station catches Mika's message: the Wren has turned back toward Pel. Its crew is safe, but the seedlings must return to storage and the research mission is cancelled.
Chief Osei says that protecting the people already on Starport Nine was a defensible choice. It doesn't feel like a victory. The empty dock bell rings once more, then never again.
You keep the old map and Mika's message. One day there may be a chance to try again—with better evidence and a little more courage.

The station continues its ordinary life: food carts rolling through the corridors, school lessons on the observation deck, Ren arguing with the vending machines. Yet every time you pass Dock Seven, the empty windows feel larger than before.

A week later Mika sends a short note from Pel. Nobody was hurt. The captain followed the safest return path and the seedlings remain in cold storage. Mika ends with a question: “If we come back when the storm is gone, will you be there?”
You reply before you have time to worry about the words. Yes. This time you will have the route ready.

ending.title: The empty docking bay
ending.note: POOR OUTCOME · The station is safe, but the ship must turn away.

illustration.alt: Rare seedlings remain inside a protected cargo case while the mission is delayed.

nodes.title: The light that lied
paragraphs: You open the hatch and follow the brightest light. For one second it looks like a clear route. Then the reflection folds, and the real ship disappears behind the ice ring.
The station's safety field slams shut. A shock travels through the outer deck. The crew evacuates and Starport Nine survives, damaged but intact. The Wren does not answer any of the rescue calls.

Search ships are launched immediately. Days later, they are still looking. Nobody says the word lost aloud, but the empty dock is quieter than it was before. The glass storm has taken the ship somewhere nobody can find.
TAVI saves the first warning in the permanent log. You listen to it once more: “Don't open the door.” Next time, you promise yourself, you will hear the whole message before you act.

After the search crews leave, the station's halls grow quiet. Nobody blames you in front of the other cadets. That is almost harder than being shouted at. You return to the first radio log and read every line without skipping the parts you wish were different.

Juno sits beside you with her old flight map. She does not tell you the choice was harmless or that the bright light fooled everyone. She asks which warning you would believe next time, and why. You start with the disconnected bell and end with the people who tried to help.

You cannot rewind this ending. The Wren remains missing, and the station has to live with the uncertainty. But the story of the warning is recorded correctly, with every detail, so that somebody else facing a bright false dock may choose better.

ending.title: The light that lied
ending.note: WORST OUTCOME · A reckless choice loses the Wren and endangers the station.

illustration.alt: A holographic view shows the station split between two futures.

nodes.act: ACT II / OUTSIDE THE STATION · 7 OF 36
nodes.title: The airlock no one uses
paragraphs: Ren leads you past the crowds sheltering in the central corridor. The last door on Deck Seven is painted a shade of orange that looks almost rude beside the station's careful blues. A label says EXTERIOR MAINTENANCE—AUTHORIZED CREW ONLY. Ren takes a key from the lining of their glove.

“I was saving this for a real emergency,” they say. “And before you ask, yes, the chief knows I borrowed it. Probably.” Their grin slips when the door opens. A thin frost clings to the inside of the airlock, although the station's temperature gauge reads normal.

You help Ren check the suit seals while TAVI speaks through your earpiece. “If you leave the station, I cannot promise what the cameras will show.” Ren snaps their helmet shut. “Then we'll have to trust what we actually touch.” For the first time tonight, that sounds like a sensible plan.

choices.label: Inspect the frozen latch
choices.detail: The cold may explain why the dock's bell rang without power.
choices.outcome: A careful scan reveals vibration marks made from the outside, not the station corridor.

choices.label: Check Ren's suit and follow
choices.detail: Keeping your teammate safe matters more than another measurement.
choices.outcome: Ren tests the seal twice and gives you a thumbs-up through the glass.

nodes.act: ACT II / OUTSIDE THE STATION · 8 OF 36
nodes.title: Walking beneath Pel
paragraphs: On the other side of the hatch there is no up or down, only the soft pull of your magnetic boots and a red planet hanging enormous beneath the station. Pel's clouds stretch across a whole hemisphere. The edge of the glass storm glitters like crushed silver foil.

Ren clips a safety line from your belt to theirs. “Rule one of spacewalking: never let the story get more interesting than your safety line.” Every few meters, a fresh alarm trembles in your headset. But this alarm is not from Starport Nine. It is the Wren's docking bell, somehow echoing through the metal under your feet.

For a moment you see a ship reflected in the station window. You turn your head; there is nothing where the ship ought to be. You understand now why the old sign warned people not to trust their eyes.

choices.label: Walk toward the reflection
choices.detail: Find a direct physical clue before the image vanishes.
choices.outcome: A scattering of silver dust clings to the outer rail in a shape like a handprint.

choices.label: Stay on the marked service rail
choices.detail: Keep both of you safely in contact with the hull.
choices.outcome: The route is slower, but Ren starts trusting your judgment in the field.

illustration.alt: Illustration from the outer-hull investigation.

nodes.act: ACT II / OUTSIDE THE STATION · 9 OF 36
nodes.title: The silent docking bell
paragraphs: The bell is exactly where Ren said it would be, behind a bolted panel on the outer wall. Its cable has been cut, capped, and tied neatly in a loop. There is no way it could be ringing.
Yet when Ren presses a gloved finger to its casing, you both feel two sharp knocks travel through the metal. Then a third. Then nothing. TAVI reports that no part of the station has moved.

Ren turns their helmet so they can look directly at you. “Somebody is knocking from the other side of tomorrow,” they say. “Are we really going to pretend this is ordinary?” You can't. But you also can't answer a knock until you know where it came from.

choices.label: Open the bell casing
choices.detail: A disconnected bell cannot hurt you—probably.
choices.outcome: Behind the casing you find a magnetic recording strip engraved with the Wren's callsign.

choices.label: Trace the knock along the hull
choices.detail: Follow the vibration, even if it takes you away from the rail.
choices.outcome: The knock travels toward an abandoned rescue buoy instead of the dock.

nodes.act: ACT II / OUTSIDE THE STATION · 10 OF 36
nodes.title: The buoy that remembered
paragraphs: The rescue buoy looks like a battered kettle floating at the end of a long steel cable. It was built to mark safe passages through the ice ring, then retired when the station received its bright new mirror system.

Its little display should be dark. Instead it shows a single line: RETURN SIGNAL ACKNOWLEDGED. The timestamp is tomorrow's date. Ren swears under their breath, not because the display is frightening but because someone has been using emergency equipment without telling the repair crew.

The buoy has enough charge for one message. Through its cracked speaker, you hear a voice repeating the same four notes as the dock bell. TAVI identifies the rhythm as an old navigator's check-in signal, one that modern pilots have almost forgotten.

choices.label: Save the old navigation pulse
choices.detail: The buoy could tell Mika which reflection is real.
choices.outcome: You copy the rhythm onto your wrist unit and label it REAL PATH.

choices.label: Give Ren the buoy's battery
choices.detail: A charge may matter more than another recording.
choices.outcome: The battery warms Ren's gloves and the station's power ledger looks less alarming.

illustration.alt: Illustration from the outer-hull investigation.

nodes.act: ACT II / OUTSIDE THE STATION · 11 OF 36
nodes.title: A message through the gloves
paragraphs: Before you can turn back, a small shape appears beyond the silver storm. It is too far away to be a spacecraft. Then it moves, and the white outline becomes the Wren's nose pointed toward Starport Nine.

Your radio hisses. A stranger whispers, “If you're outside, don't look directly at the bright dock.” You try to answer, but your transmitter reports that the message hasn't been sent yet. Ren puts one gloved hand against yours; the contact gives you a steadiness that the safety line alone couldn't provide.

Another reflection blooms in the distance: two stations, two docks, and the same little ship flying between them. You realize the Wren may have to decide which Starport to believe—and that the choice could depend on what you bring back.
By the time you reenter the airlock, your visor has a scratch shaped like a lightning bolt. Nothing else on the suit was touched. You decide not to mention that part to TAVI until you understand it.

choices.label: Keep the visor scratch as evidence
choices.detail: There is a physical mark that could be compared with the lost minute.
choices.outcome: TAVI records the scratch and starts matching it to the strange sensor data.

choices.label: Tell Chief Osei what Ren saw
choices.detail: A second witness might convince the station to listen.
choices.outcome: The chief asks both of you to report to Control immediately.

nodes.act: ACT III / JUNO'S FLIGHT SCHOOL · 13 OF 36
nodes.title: The pilot who stopped flying
paragraphs: Pilot Juno lives in a room overlooking the service hangar. It is filled with paper maps, tea cups, and a broken flight stick that has clearly been repaired more times than it should. She does not seem surprised when you mention the disappearing minute.

“The mirror was supposed to make us safer,” she says, pulling a folded chart from a drawer. “Before it, a pilot could choose where to look. After it, the beam did the looking for us.” She sets down a photograph of a much younger Juno beside a damaged rescue shuttle. The photograph shows no casualties, but the shuttle's cracked window is enough to explain why Juno never flew that route again.

You tell her about the Wren. She listens as though your voice is part of a conversation she has been expecting for years. “Then we have a chance to make the right mistake,” she says. “First we'll need to find out which of the two routes is real.”

choices.label: Ask Juno to tell the whole story
choices.detail: A mistake from the past might be a lesson for tomorrow.
choices.outcome: Juno reveals that the mirror once pointed toward an image of home instead of the station.

choices.label: Ask Juno to take the controls
choices.detail: A practiced hand is worth more than an old map.
choices.outcome: Juno follows you to the simulator and promises she won't abandon the Wren.

illustration.alt: Illustrated scene aboard Starport Nine's old flight simulator.

nodes.act: ACT III / JUNO'S FLIGHT SCHOOL · 14 OF 36
nodes.title: A flight with no window
paragraphs: Juno leads you into a tiny training cockpit whose windows have been painted black. Three switches are missing their labels. The seat belt is held together with a strip of bright yellow tape that says DO NOT WORRY. You worry anyway.

“In a glass storm, a pretty picture can be a trap,” she says. “Good pilots learn what their ship is telling them before they ask their eyes.” She turns on the training alarm. The simulator shakes. The screen offers two different docking approaches, both labelled SAFE.

Outside the cockpit, you can hear evacuees talking in the corridor. Their voices make this feel less like a game. Somewhere in tomorrow's real cockpit, Mika will face the same impossible pair of routes. You put a hand on the unlabeled switches and begin.

choices.label: Navigate from the instruments
choices.detail: Use distance, gravity and radio timing instead of the glowing arrows.
choices.outcome: The simulated Wren reaches the true dock without ever seeing it.

choices.label: Navigate by Juno's spoken count
choices.detail: Let the pilot talk you through the storm one turn at a time.
choices.outcome: Your course is less precise, but you and Juno learn to move as a team.

nodes.act: ACT III / JUNO'S FLIGHT SCHOOL · 15 OF 36
nodes.title: The route under the route
paragraphs: Your first training run ends with a jolt and a splash of imaginary orange warning lights. Juno reaches over and turns the screen off. “There,” she says, pointing not at the image but at the old paper map beside your knee. “A docking path has a shape. If the shape changes, somebody is lying.”

Under a smudge in the map's corner you find a thin yellow line. It loops below the station and returns from the dark side of the ice ring. A modern navigation computer would never choose it. It is slow, wastes fuel, and offers almost no view of the dock.

Juno says that is exactly why it worked. In a storm full of false lights, the safest course is sometimes the least beautiful one. You can hear TAVI calculating how long it would take the Wren to follow the yellow line.

choices.label: Memorize the forgotten approach
choices.detail: Keep the whole path in your head in case screens fail.
choices.outcome: You can now describe a safe route without looking at a single light.

choices.label: Ask Juno to radio her old crew
choices.detail: People who used this route may know its hidden hazards.
choices.outcome: Two retired pilots reply, and the crew gains a plan they can trust.

nodes.act: ACT III / JUNO'S FLIGHT SCHOOL · 16 OF 36
nodes.title: One more chair
paragraphs: Juno opens the cockpit door to find Mika's voice spilling from the hallway speakers. “I can't make the left turn,” Mika says. “The bright dock is pulling the instruments toward it.” Juno freezes. She recognizes the words.

“That's what I told my instructor before the rescue shuttle hit the ring,” she says. The admission costs her something. You think of the old photograph and the fact that Juno kept the broken flight stick instead of throwing it away.
You have an opportunity to ask what happened next. But the radio is still open, and Mika can hear every word. You can protect Juno's privacy or give Mika the warning that might help them survive.

choices.label: Ask Juno to speak directly to Mika
choices.detail: The pilot's painful experience may make the right difference.
choices.outcome: Juno's voice steadies on the third sentence: 'Ignore the bright one. Fly the shape.'

choices.label: Describe the simulator mistake yourself
choices.detail: You can explain the danger without exposing Juno's past.
choices.outcome: Mika copies the instrument-only approach while Juno nods her approval.

illustration.alt: Illustrated scene aboard Starport Nine's old flight simulator.

nodes.act: ACT III / JUNO'S FLIGHT SCHOOL · 17 OF 36
nodes.title: The yellow line
paragraphs: Your next attempt is quieter. No rattling cockpit. No simulated emergency. Just the yellow route on the old map and a fading voice from a ship that technically has not launched yet.

Juno asks whether you would rather be famous for bringing the Wren home or useful to the people who need it. You have no trouble answering. You came here because someone had to answer a message, not because you wanted your face on a station bulletin.

Before you leave, Juno hands you the broken flight stick. It is heavier than it looks. “Keep it until the Wren lands,” she says. “Then we'll fix it together.” A small gesture, but it feels like being trusted with a whole history.
The pilot's route is slower than the mirror route and may never fix the time loop. But you finally understand how a real ship can reach a real station without trusting a single reflection.

choices.label: Put the yellow route in TAVI's memory
choices.detail: The computer should know what the crew knows.
choices.outcome: TAVI saves the approach and promises not to replace it with a prettier one.

choices.label: Ask Juno to join the bridge team
choices.detail: An old pilot and a young cadet might make a good crew.
choices.outcome: She walks with you to Control carrying the map under one arm.

nodes.act: ACT IV / INSIDE THE ECHO · 19 OF 36
